hub.intro: Five places in Signal City. Two are open tonight; the rest are built out in the full version. Pick where you want to start.

locations.name: The Wire
locations.teaches: An anonymous leak nobody can date. Who benefits if you believe it before it is checked?

locations.name: The Operator
locations.teaches: Fifty accounts, one operator. Telling coordinated noise from an actual crowd.

locations.name: The Outbreak
locations.teaches: Health advice in a crisis, moving faster than anyone can correct it.

profile.skillsNote: All five are shown whether you have earned them or not. Two missions are playable tonight, so this is the shape of the whole game, not a scoreboard.
profile.noBadges: No badges yet. Finish a mission and one lands here.

skills.name: STOP
skills.teaches: Notice the pull to pass something on, and pause before you do.
skills.how: Reach an ending without sharing the post first.

skills.name: VERIFY
skills.teaches: Trace a claim back to where it actually started.
skills.how: Find every piece of evidence a mission holds.

skills.name: QUESTION
skills.teaches: Ask a confident answer where it got that.
skills.how: Ask NOVA for her source instead of taking her word.

skills.name: DISCERN
skills.teaches: Tell real footage from a real lie. The cut is the edit.
skills.how: Find the full recording in The Copy.

skills.name: RESPOND
skills.teaches: Say what is known and what is not, to the people who saw it.
skills.how: Post a correction at the end of a mission.

teacher.preview: Concept preview — not a working feature

teacher.metricsLabel: Where the class is strong, and where it isn't
teacher.privacy: Teachers see learning patterns across a class. They never see an individual student's private decisions — what one student chose inside a mission stays with that student.
teacher.planHint: Open any figure to see what this class would be assigned next.
teacher.readingLabel: What a teacher would do with this
teacher.reading: Uncertainty handling sits lowest at 43%, which usually means a class is guessing confidently rather than saying it does not know. That is the lesson to plan next, not the one they scored highest on.

metrics.plan: Strong, and it was practised: the evidence board in The Exam Rumour is source verification with the steps named. Stretch it with the upload chain in The Copy, where the first account to post is not the source.
metrics.label: Source verification

metrics.plan: The number most often overestimated, by classes and teachers both. Have them ask NOVA for her source in either mission, then compare what she claimed before the question with what she admits after it.
metrics.label: AI literacy

metrics.plan: The highest figure here and the most dangerous one. The Copy exists for this class: a group confident in its eyes stops checking where a video came from, and the clip in that mission is genuine.
metrics.label: Visual verification

metrics.plan: Middling. Ask who benefits from each claim in The Exam Rumour, including the accounts that shared it in good faith, and who is not in the room to answer.
metrics.label: Bias recognition

metrics.plan: The lowest, which usually means a class guesses confidently rather than saying it does not know. Run The Exam Rumour and require 'I still don't know' as an ending, then discuss out loud what that honesty cost and what it saved.
metrics.label: Uncertainty handling

hero.sub: About the post on this page — believed it or dismissed it, in under a second, without checking a thing. RE:AL is a game about the ninety seconds you skipped.
hero.playNote: Two missions · four minutes · no sign-up

problem.label: The problem
problem.statement: Nothing about it is obviously wrong.
problem.body: That is what makes it work. A claim does not spread because people are careless — it spreads because checking costs time and believing costs nothing. Forty-seven thousand people passed this one on before anyone opened the school's website.
problem.second: And the confirmation arrives before the correction does.
problem.note: Both posts are the real thing, from Mission 01, rendered by the component the game uses.

check.label: Checking it
check.statement: So you check it. Here is what that costs.
check.lead: The marker above is the game's own. It moves as you read, because this is the loop: see it, question it, investigate it, decide, and live with the decision.

beats.title: Ask the AI and it answers immediately
beats.body: NOVA is fluent, confident and cites nothing. Ask her where she got it and the number moves — that drop is the entire argument about AI in one screen.
beats.note: Her confidence, as the game draws it. 62% before the question, 34% after.

beats.title: Trace it yourself and it takes work
beats.body: Seven slots on a corkboard. Three can be found tonight; the other four say plainly that they are not built. Each one names the skill it just taught you.

beats.title: And looking harder does not always help
beats.body: In the second mission the video is genuine. The lighting is consistent, the lip sync holds, and NOVA says so correctly. It was filmed at a different meeting a year earlier, and the sentence before it is missing.
beats.note: The clip from The Copy. Nothing in the frame carries a date.

check.spreadTitle: Skip all of it, and this is what you did
check.spreadBody: Share without checking and the game does not mark you wrong. It shows you your own post leaving your hands.
check.spreadNote: Six copies, sixty milliseconds apart, your handle on every one. Trust 82% → 21%. Reach 63% → 96%.

close.statement: Two minutes. One claim. Your name on whatever happens next.
close.body: It runs in a browser, needs no account, and stores nothing beyond the tab you have open. Two missions are playable; three more worlds are named in the city and say honestly that they are not built yet.
close.playNote: Starts on the same screen you just saw
close.footer: 1 of 40 planned missions. The Mission Builder lets students write their own.
